sessions.title: Agents-from-zero onboarding (English and Hindi)
sessions.description: New to AI agents? Start here. This beginner workshop runs in English and Hindi and takes you from "what is an agent" to building and running a simple one yourself. Naina Sachdev, India Chapter Lead at Dev3pack and an AI engineer who builds multi-agent systems, guides you step by step, with no prior agent experience needed. Bring a laptop. You leave with a working agent and the vocabulary to follow the rest of the week, from payments to identity and trust.

sessions.title: Opening hour: meet and greet and StackChan robot demo
sessions.description: Kick off the Agents Hub with a relaxed first hour. Meet the hub team and the other builders, see the StackChan robot demo, and look at the empty agent stack map on the whiteboard. Over the week every session adds a piece to the map, from identity and payments to trust and disputes. The hub is a small community space with no stage, so come in, ask questions and find the people working on what you care about. Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva, who works in developer relations on agentic payments, hosts.

sessions.title: x402 and ERC-8183: what works today and what is on the roadmap
sessions.description: x402 lets a service charge an AI agent per request over plain HTTP. ERC-8183 is a newer standard for agents hiring each other with escrowed payment. Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva, developer relations engineer and writer on agentic payments, gives a ten-minute reality check: what each standard is for, what already runs in production, and what upstream has not shipped yet. A quick orientation for anyone who wants to know which pieces they can build on today.

sessions.title: ERC-8004 in practice: registration works, reputation is the hard part
sessions.description: ERC-8004 gives AI agents an onchain identity and a place for reputation. Registering an agent is easy. Making reputation mean something is not. Fortunato Cinquepalmi, Product Lead at Kleros, explains why the identity side works, why scores are easy to game, and why top-ranked agents often have little product behind them. A ten-minute talk for builders deciding whether to trust an agent score.

sessions.title: Agent payments with real users: three live examples
sessions.description: Plenty of agent payment demos exist. Few have real users. Lena Hierzi, DevRel Lead at Celo Core Co, shows three agent payment setups that people actually use, how to tell them apart from test traffic and wash trading, and which parts a builder can copy for their own project. Ten minutes, with examples you can look up afterwards.

sessions.title: Will agent payments stick?
sessions.description: Agent payment rails keep shipping, but is anyone using them? Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva moderates Fortunato Cinquepalmi (Kleros) and Lena Hierzi (Celo Core Co) as optimists and sceptics argue the case for x402, ERC-8004 and plain card payments. Where is real demand, what is hype, and what would change your mind? Halfway through, the room helps fill in the agent stack map on the whiteboard. Expect disagreement and questions from the audience.

sessions.title: Follow the money: reading on-chain agent payment data
sessions.description: Agent payment headlines are huge, while real usage is much smaller. This hands-on workshop teaches a practical method for reading on-chain agent payment data. Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva, who writes about agentic payments, shows how to find the real buyers and sellers, spot repeated counterparties, bot-driven volume and hackathon or test traffic, and judge what a believable volume number looks like. Then you pair up, pick a chain or facilitator, and classify its top payers and sellers as real, bot or test. Bring a laptop.

sessions.title: Signed Is Not Authorized: a live, bounded user mandate inside an x402 payment
sessions.description: A signature proves a key signed. It does not prove you allow this action now, within these limits. When an agent pays or decides for you, the question is on whose authority. Anantha Krishnan, founder of Sarva Labs and the MOI protocol, shows how authority can be held as live state, and what an x402 payment looks like when it carries a mandate that only the participant can change. Useful for anyone designing how agents get permission to spend.

sessions.title: 8004, x402, AP2, ACP and MPP disambiguated, and why not just give the agent a card?
sessions.description: Five agent standards, overlapping names and a lot of confusion. This workshop works from open questions posted by builders. Lena Hierzi (Celo Core Co) and Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva sort the standards by the job they do, identity, payment or checkout, then walk three common setups: an agent paying for an API, an agent buying from a merchant, and an agent hiring another agent. It closes on a question many builders ask: if you can issue an agent a card, why give it a wallet? Bring your own questions.

sessions.title: Memory your agent owns, with Swarm MCP
sessions.description: Most agents keep their memory in a vendor's database or lose it between sessions. Andrá Aráyi, CTO at Solar Punk, shows how the Swarm MCP server gives any MCP-compatible agent persistent memory that the agent owner controls, stored on the decentralised Swarm network. Live demo: an agent keeps a logbook, you see what it wrote, and the memory survives a restart. MCP is the open protocol agents use to call tools. Good for builders who want portable, user-owned agent state.

sessions.title: Evidence has a shelf life: queryable, expiring data for ERC-8004 agents
sessions.description: ERC-8004 stores hashes onchain but leaves the actual evidence offchain, with no rule on how long it stays available. Shantelle Awomoyi, Head of Ecosystem at Golem Factory, shows how Arkiv, a queryable data layer for Ethereum, lets agents keep validation payloads and coordination state as wallet-owned data. Each record is checked against its onchain hash and expires on a schedule you set. Learn how to keep agent evidence verifiable without keeping it forever.

sessions.title: Packaged skills that let any agent use a complex protocol correctly
sessions.description: Agents often misuse complex protocols because they lack context. Packaged skills fix that by bundling instructions, examples and checks that any agent can load. Andrá Aráyi, CTO at Solar Punk, and Levente Kiss use the open-source Swarm skills library as a case study: how a skill is structured, how an agent picks it up, and how to publish one for your own protocol. A ten-minute talk for builders who want agents to use their tools correctly.

sessions.title: Evidence under the payment: who asked, who served, what it cost, signed by both sides
sessions.description: When an agent pays another agent, who can later prove what happened? Steven Mih, founder and CEO of Action State Group and a maintainer of Mesh-LLM, shows an open-source evidence layer for agent payments. Both sides seal every exchange, paid or not, as a signed, hash-chained record that any third party can verify offline. Start with a 60-second live demo on a running mesh of inference nodes, then get hands-on, with places for up to 15 attendees.

sessions.title: Lexon, deterministic AI
sessions.description: Language models are fluent but unpredictable. Henning Diedrich, creator of the plain-text smart contract language Lexon and head of protocol at Swarm, presents small language models built on symbolic AI that behave as deterministically as a programming language. He live-codes a hybrid workflow that combines generative and symbolic AI, so every step stays transparent and checkable. For anyone who needs agents whose decisions can be explained.

sessions.title: Networking and agent competition
sessions.description: Wind down the first day with the other builders. Compare notes on what you heard, add what you learned to the hub knowledge base by scanning the Bonfires QR code, and follow the agent competition live on the hub TV. No agenda, no stage, just a small room full of people building with agents. Paul Lange from Celo engineering runs the competition. A good moment to find collaborators for the rest of the week.

sessions.title: Agents-from-zero onboarding
sessions.description: New to AI agents? Start here. This beginner workshop takes you from "what is an agent" to building and running a simple one yourself. Naina Sachdev (India Chapter Lead at Dev3pack) and Gopika Chauhan (Dev3pack, IIT Mandi) guide you step by step, with no prior agent experience needed. Bring a laptop. You leave with a working agent and the vocabulary to follow the rest of the week, from payments to identity and trust.

sessions.title: x402 beyond USDC: Paying an agent in USD₮ and USA₮
sessions.description: Watch an agent pay for a service through x402 and see the payment settle live on screen. First with a regular stablecoin, then with USD₮, and with USA₮ if it is live by then. Lena Hierzi, DevRel Lead at Celo Core Co, who works on bringing regulated local stablecoins into agent payments, narrates each step: what the agent sends, what the service checks and what lands on chain. Ten minutes, and you can repeat it yourself afterwards.

sessions.title: How x402 settles beyond USDC: permit, ERC-20 and local stablecoins
sessions.description: x402 started with USDC, but agents will pay in many tokens. Vedant Anand, co-founder of Bags and a maintainer of the x402 protocol, explains how settlement works for tokens other than USDC. He covers EIP-2612 permit payments, plain ERC-20 transfers and what a local stablecoin needs to be supported. Based on his merged x402 work, with practical advice for builders who want their API to accept more than one currency.

sessions.title: Agent Vault: the portable login and payments layer for your AI assistants
sessions.description: Mainstream adoption of agentic payments is held back by trust and security: card details can leak, and agents can go rogue and overspend. Kartik Mehta, Solutions Engineer at Self Labs, a zero-knowledge identity and proof-of-humanity protocol, explains the main challenges with agentic payments today and how Self built Agent Vault, a portable login and payments layer for your AI assistants, to address them. Learn where agent card payments stand and how they compare with x402, then join an open discussion on which to use for which job.

sessions.title: Pricing and treasury for a machine
sessions.description: An agent that sells a service must decide what to charge, in which currency, and how much risk to hold. Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva, who writes about agentic payments, gives a ten-minute introduction to pricing and treasury for a machine: setting prices in stablecoins, keeping a budget and reserves, and what changes when no human reviews each sale. Sets up the roundtable that follows.

sessions.title: Price feeds and stablecoin pegs
sessions.description: An agent that pays or prices in stablecoins needs a price it can trust, and a stablecoin is only worth one dollar if its peg holds. Aditya Arora explains where agents can get reliable prices, how price feeds track stablecoin pegs, and what an agent should do when the feed and the market disagree. Ten minutes for builders who automate payments or treasury.

sessions.title: Paying in an ecosystem stablecoin over x402
sessions.description: Not every agent will pay in USDC. Daniel Ortega shows what it takes to accept and pay with an ecosystem stablecoin over x402, using USDG on Arbitrum as the example. Ten minutes on how the token settles, what a builder needs to change in an x402 setup, and where the trade-offs sit compared with the largest stablecoins.

sessions.title: Stablecoins as unit of account: whose money is it?
sessions.description: When the payer is software, who absorbs a freeze or a depeg? Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva moderates Aditya Arora and Daniel Ortega on issuer risk, freezes and the choice of currency for pricing an agent service. Should an agent price in dollars, a local currency or whatever it holds? Bring your own case: the audience joins the discussion, and the group fills in the payments part of the whiteboard map.

sessions.title: Security Risks in x402 Agentic Payments and How to Prevent Them
sessions.description: AI agents can pay for online services with x402. Mistakes can mean lost money, the same payment happening twice, or a service used without being paid. Zuhaib, co-founder of Slot Zero Security and a smart contract security researcher, explains five common risks with practical examples, and what developers can do to stop abuse and handle failed payments safely. Useful for anyone running an agent that spends or an API that charges.

sessions.title: FX over x402 and shared liquidity
sessions.description: Paying across currencies is a foreign exchange problem in disguise. S Rithik Kumar (COO) and Yudhisthra (CTO) of Aqua0 show how FX between stablecoins can run inside an x402 payment, using shared liquidity across DEX pools: the agent pays in a euro stablecoin and the service receives USDC. Learn why thin liquidity breaks cross-currency agent payments and how one deposit can back many pools at once.

sessions.title: The last mile into INR and EUR: from stablecoin to local money
sessions.description: A payment is only finished when someone can spend the money. Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva and S Rithik Kumar follow a payment from Mumbai to Spain: where the exchange rate comes from, what happens at the off-ramp into rupees or euros, and what still breaks. The session also wraps up the payments sessions by completing the Mumbai to Spain payment on the whiteboard map with the room.

sessions.title: Permissioned wallets for agents: scoped, revocable allowances with ERC-7715 and ERC-7710
sessions.description: How do you let an agent spend without handing over your keys? Ayush Bherwani, Senior DevRel Engineer at MetaMask, shows how ERC-7715 and ERC-7710 let a user grant an agent a capped, time-limited and revocable allowance from their own smart account. See what a permission request looks like, how an agent redeems it, and how you take it back at any time. For builders giving agents limited spending power.

sessions.title: Selling to agents: how an agent finds a service and pays per call
sessions.description: Can software become your customer? Viral Sangani, co-founder and CTO at Cesto and builder of usebuy.ai, shows an agent that finds a service, gets a quote and pays per call in stablecoins on Celo, with no account, API key or subscription. See what the seller has to publish so agents can discover and trust it, and what that means for pricing. For anyone who wants to sell to agents.

sessions.title: Building agent products with a small team
sessions.description: Agents changed how a small team can ship a consumer product. Ankit Tailor, founding engineer at Cesto, whose apps have handled over 100 million onchain transactions, shares how his team uses agents to build faster, what makes an agent feature feel simple to users, and what still needs a human. For product builders deciding where agents belong in their workflow.

sessions.title: Designing agents that act on real assets
sessions.description: Once an agent can trade or move assets, design decisions become safety decisions. Victor Muñz, developer relations at Flare who also builds multi-agent trading and payment systems, covers permissions, visibility and keeping users in control when agents act on real assets. Learn how to make agent actions understandable before they happen, and easy to stop. Leaves time for questions from the room.

sessions.title: Your Next Customer Won't Click: Designing for Humans and Agents
sessions.description: Your next customer may arrive as an agent that never opens your homepage. Can it discover your offer, understand the price, get permission and pay, or does your product stop at a login screen? Fortunato Cinquepalmi, Product Lead at Kleros, looks at CLI, API and Markdown as product surfaces, and why people still need images, comparisons and clear decisions. Leave knowing what the agent should do, what the human should see and where trust must be earned.

sessions.title: Can an Agent Buy From You? Find, Check, Pay, Get the Result
sessions.description: Can an unfamiliar agent arrive at your service and become a paying customer? Harish Kotra, developer relations specialist, follows one agent from an llms.txt file to an MCP tool, an ERC-8004 registration check, an x402 payment and a returned result. Then he inspects the interface contract: typed inputs, versions, review and rollback. Ends with open discussion with Fortunato Cinquepalmi. Bring an API you want agents to use.

sessions.title: Networking and agent competition
sessions.description: Close the day with the other builders. Compare notes on the payments sessions, add what you learned to the hub knowledge base by scanning the Bonfires QR code, follow the agent competition on the hub TV and try a live x402 payment at the chai vending demo. A small room, no stage, and a good time to find collaborators. Paul Lange from Celo engineering runs the competition.

Naina Sachdev (India Chapter Lead at Dev3pack) and Gopika Chauhan (Dev3pack, IIT Mandi) guide you step by step, with no prior agent experience needed. Bring a laptop. You leave with a working agent and the vocabulary to follow the rest of the week, including identity and trust.

sessions.title: What ERC-8004 actually means: identity, reputation and validation in practice
sessions.description: ERC-8004 gives AI agents an identity, a place for reputation and a way to validate their work. Registering an agent is easy. Making reputation mean something is the hard part. Lena Hierzi (Celo Core Co) and Fortunato Cinquepalmi (Kleros) walk through the three registries and a real registration, and ask: after an agent is paid through x402, can the service leave feedback, and how would a reputation network grow from that? Harpreet Singh (Namespace, ENS) covers agent identity with ENS names. Finish with open discussion and a hands-on step: register or read an agent live.

sessions.title: Reputation-system failure modes: sybils, review farming, whitewashing
sessions.description: Open agent economies run on reputation, and reputation is the first thing attackers farm. This roundtable maps three classic failure modes: sybil identities minted at machine speed, review farming with wash-traded feedback, and whitewashing, where a bad actor burns an identity and starts fresh. YQ (founder of AltLayer and 8004scan), Steven Mih (Action State Group), Andrá Aráyi and Andrei Mitrea (Solar Punk) compare defences: payment-gated feedback, identity cost and stake, weighted scoring and verifiable evidence on durable storage.

sessions.title: How agents find and pay for services
sessions.description: How does an agent find a service it can trust, and pay for it? Viral Sangani (Cesto, usebuy.ai) shows pay-per-call buying in practice, including discovery, quotes and receipts. Vedant Anand (Bags, x402 maintainer) explains how x402 settles for tokens beyond USDC. Twenty minutes that connect finding a service with paying for it, and set up the live demo later in the day.

sessions.title: Agent communication: A2A, MCP and how agents agree on meaning
sessions.description: MCP lets an agent call tools and A2A lets agents talk to each other, but a working connection does not guarantee shared meaning. Harish Kotra, developer relations specialist, shows why an explicit agreement about what a tool means and returns matters, with typed contracts as the fix. Learn how to make your agent interface checkable by another agent.

sessions.title: How agents are found by domain, and where identity fits in
sessions.description: Before an agent can be trusted, someone has to find it. Lena Hierzi, DevRel Lead at Celo Core Co, shows how agents can be discovered through domain names, and how identity, including ERC-8004 registration, fits on top of that. Learn how a buyer links a domain to an agent and what proof that link gives you. A short talk that leads into the live demo that follows.

sessions.title: Agents: who are we dealing with, and what did we buy?
sessions.description: An agent finds a service, pays for it and returns an answer. What would make you trust the result? Lena Hierzi (Celo Core Co) reads the agent's ERC-8004 identity and reputation record, discovers a service from the usebuy.ai side, and follows an x402 purchase on Celo. Then she inspects the receipt and discusses what feedback a paid interaction can support. Part one of a live, three-part workflow from identity to resolution.

sessions.title: Agents × UPI: what machine payments can learn from UPI
sessions.description: UPI won because India treated the payment rail as shared, open infrastructure and let apps compete on top. Agents now pay for services and for each other with no human confirming each step. What should machine payments copy from UPI? Deon Menezes, Piyush Maheshwari (Moi) and Naina Sachdev (Dev3pack) discuss shared rails, interoperability, scoped delegation and mandates that can be changed in real time, and what happens after the spend: proving a payment matched its mandate, settling disputes and receipts that reconcile.

sessions.title: Who Gets Sued When the Agent Makes a Mistake? How to get prepared in a decentralized way with KYC and arbitration
sessions.description: An agent buys a service. The payment succeeds. The work is disputed, and nobody can show who authorized the deal. This session from the Agents ×Legal hub puts one case through the whole chain: the person or company behind the agent, its delegated mandate, the policy checks, the promised delivery and the remedy. The room changes the facts: a revoked mandate, an eligible recipient but an unauthorized purpose, or a paid service that fails its specification. Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva and Facundo Trotz lead.

sessions.title: Markets Humans Ignore: Economic Mechanisms for AI Agents
sessions.description: Some economic mechanisms look elegant on paper and attract few people: the reward is too small, the task too repetitive, the decision too slow. What changes when the participant is an AI agent? Cléent Lesaege, CTO and founder of Kleros and Seer, uses prediction markets, curated information and dispute evaluation as examples to examine the cost of taking part, the reward for useful work and the penalty for being wrong.

sessions.title: Networking and agent competition
sessions.description: Wrap up the identity and trust sessions with the other builders. Compare notes on what you saw in the live demo, add what you learned to the hub knowledge base by scanning the Bonfires QR code, follow the agent competition on the hub TV and try a live x402 payment at the chai vending demo. A small room, no stage. Paul Lange from Celo engineering runs the competition.

sessions.description: New to AI agents? Start here. This beginner workshop takes you from "what is an agent" to building and running a simple one yourself. Lena Hierzi, DevRel Lead at Celo Core Co, guides you step by step, with no prior agent experience needed. Bring a laptop. You leave with a working agent and the vocabulary to follow the day, from machine payments to authority and trust.

sessions.title: Machines that pay: robotics and agent payments
sessions.description: What changes when a robot or other machine pays for things itself? Nicolá Arnedo Villanueva, who writes about agentic payments, opens the community day with a talk on robotics and agent payments: what a machine needs to buy a service, who authorizes the spend, and where the first real use cases appear. Followed by community sessions chosen on the whiteboard. Come with your own examples.

sessions.title: From discovery to dispute: equip your agent or marketplace to scale
sessions.description: Build the part of your agent business that turns interest into paid work, and a bad experience into a customer you can recover. Bring an agent, API or marketplace idea. Fortunato Cinquepalmi, Product Lead at Kleros, leads the group in picking one and designing its full customer journey on the whiteboard: get discovered through credible profiles, earn trust with verifiable claims, take x402 payments, define delivery, and handle dissatisfaction through support, refunds and independent dispute resolution. Leave with a customer-flow map, policy requirements and public code links.

sessions.title: Who Answered Your Prompt? The issues in modern inference
sessions.description: When you call an AI API, you trust a black box: which model ran, who served it, and whether it was swapped, quantized or censored on the way. Ofir Eliasi, CTO of Lava Network, which builds secure routing for AI inference, unpacks the hidden trust gaps in modern inference and reviews emerging fixes, from cryptographic proofs to decentralized provider networks, that make every answer accountable. For anyone building on third-party models.

sessions.title: Giving agents authority you can revoke: the Moi layer in action
sessions.description: What does it look like when an agent acts for you on authority you can take back? Anantha Krishnan, founder of Sarva Labs and the MOI protocol, and Piyush Maheshwari (Moi) show the Moi authority layer in action: an agent acts only on a live, bounded mandate from the person it works for, and only that person can change it. Follow how transactions run through agents on Ethereum and see a mandate being narrowed and revoked.

sessions.title: Competition finals and hub wrap
sessions.description: The finals of the hub competitions and a wrap-up of the week.

sessions.title: Agents: when the payment goes wrong, a dispute signal and tamper-evident memory on Swarm
sessions.description: What happens when a paid agent job goes wrong? Andrá Aráyi, CTO at Solar Punk, stages a failed or contested purchase and shows a demo dispute signal linked to the transaction. He records the event and its logs on Swarm, then retrieves and verifies the evidence and compares a tampered copy with the original. Then the room changes the story: alter a reputation signal, a payment fact or a memory entry, and vote by QR to see which signals changed your confidence. Leave with the whole workflow, from identity to resolution, and an open-source demo to adapt.

sessions.title: Accounts for agents: smart accounts, EIP-7702 and interop, and what is still unsolved
sessions.description: Agent wallets sit on top of Ethereum accounts, and accounts are changing. Mislav, researcher at Ethlabs and former CEO of the interop protocol Klaster, explains how smart accounts and EIP-7702 let a normal address behave like a programmable one, how this helps across chains, and which problems are still open for agents. A practical view of what the account layer can and cannot do today.

sessions.title: Who holds the keys? Wallets, permissions and accounts for agents, a moderated panel
sessions.description: Self-custody, smart accounts, delegated permissions: which approach should an agent use, and who is responsible when it goes wrong? Lena Hierzi (Celo Core Co) moderates Mislav (Ethlabs) and Ayush Bherwani (MetaMask) in a frank comparison of when to use which, with questions from the room. Leave with a clearer rule of thumb for giving agents money without giving them your keys.

sessions.title: Your Path Into Ethereum ecosystem with EIP Hub
How Fast Is Your Client? Benchmarking the Ethereum Execution Layer for Glamsterdam
sessions.description: Glamsterdam raises Ethereum's gas limit from 60M to 200M and reprices EVM operations, so every gas cost has to match how long clients actually take to execute it. We walk through the pipeline that measures this end to end: designing benchmarks that isolate single operations, running them on realistic state across all execution clients with benchmarkoor, and replaying the same workloads on devnets and mainnet shadow forks to confirm the results hold on a live network.

sessions.title: EIP Selection to Support Fast Fork Cadence

sessions.title: EIP Signal Quiz Game - Understanding EIPs

sessions.title: EIP-8184: LUCID Encrypted Mempool

sessions.title: The Price Is Right: Setting Gas Prices for Glamsterdam
sessions.description: This talk explores the methodology behind Glamsterdam’s gas repricing work, using EIP-8038 and EIP-2780 to explain how synthetic block testing, cross-client measurements, resource decomposition, and conservative assumptions translate throughput targets into gas costs and shape the final pricing model.

sessions.title: Frame txs & private payments: EIP-8141 in practice

sessions.description: Ethereum now has multiple paths toward post-quantum security, from lattice-based cryptography and EIP-7885 to hash-based signatures combined with proof aggregation. This talk compares these approaches through their performance, standardization, cryptographic assumptions, and the additional complexity introduced by specialized signature schemes and aggregation layers such as EIP-8288.

sessions.title: EIP Signal Quiz Game - Protocol & Core Ethereum

sessions.title: The Token Is Standardised. The Institution Isn't: Where Should Ethereum Standards Stop?

The difficult part starts when that asset has investors with different eligibility, jurisdictions, compliance requirements, custody arrangements and transfer rules. I want to look at what standards such as ERC-3643 and ERC-7943 are getting right, where they still leave gaps, and whether we are standardising the right layer of institutional finance.

sessions.title: Building Trustless Systems, Together

sessions.title: EIP-7702 in Practice for Dapps

sessions.title: Are Confidential Tokens Ready for Enterprise Payments?

sessions.description: Every token makes a claim: ownership, access, a share of cashflow, a vote. This session sets the shared vocabulary for the whole hub. sessions.title: Nobody Votes. Can Better Deliberation Fix It?
sessions.description: Most token holders skip the vote because it costs more time & attention than it returns. Civic tech has been working on the same problem in cities and citizen assemblies, using deliberation tools that find where people agree before anything goes to a vote. This session looks at how those tools work, what they have changed in public decision-making, and what DAOs can borrow from them.

sessions.title: Optimistic Governance: From Vote to Veto
sessions.description: In optimistic governance, a proposal passes by default unless holders object within a set window. The holder’s right shifts from voting yes or no to blocking what they disagree with. That lowers the turnout problem, but it raises new questions: who is watching when nobody votes, how high should the veto bar be, and what stops a team from passing things quietly? This session covers how the model works, where it is already in use, and what holders give up and gain when silence counts as consent.

sessions.title: From Tribe to Agent
sessions.description: People have always built institutions to coordinate, hold assets and make decisions together. What changes when those decisions are made by software? This opening talk traces the path from human communities to DAOs and agentic organisations, asking which foundations still matter: identity, shared rules, recognised authority and someone who answers when things go wrong.

sessions.title: Who Do You Sue?
sessions.description: An agent signs a deal, moves funds or causes a loss. Who does the other party bring a claim against, and where? This roundtable follows a dispute from identifying the responsible party to choosing a forum and enforcing a decision. We’ll examine what contracts, registries and onchain arbitration can resolve, and where accountability still breaks down.

sessions.title: The Public Round Is Back: Raising Onchain in 2026
sessions.description: Raising from a community puts difficult questions back on the table: what is being sold, what rights come with it, and who is accountable after the raise? This roundtable examines public token fundraising through investor protection, disclosure, access restrictions and treasury governance. What would a public round need to get right to earn lasting trust?

sessions.title: Community Fishbowl
sessions.description: Bring a live problem from something you’re building, advising or governing. This open discussion gives the room a chance to test ideas against practical experience, from agent permissions and DAO disputes to privacy and entity formation. Participants rotate through the conversation, with an open chair for anyone who can sharpen the question or offer a useful counterexample.

sessions.title: Paid in Dollars, Taxed in Rupees: What Breaks for Indian Founders, and what Actually Works?
sessions.description: Your work is global, your payment arrives in dollars or stablecoins, and your tax obligations remain local. For people working from India, this roundtable explores how employment, contracting and token compensation create different questions around income, valuation, reporting and cross-border payments. What records and arrangements should be in place before the first payment arrives?

sessions.title: Who Owns the Upside When the Founder is an Agent?
sessions.description: An agent creates a product, earns revenue and reinvests the proceeds. Who should own the business, and who can claim what it produces? This roundtable separates ownership, control and economic rights, examining the competing claims of developers, operators, funders and users. We’ll ask how those rights could be documented, changed and enforced as the agent becomes more autonomous.

sessions.title: Agents & Personhood
sessions.description: Does an autonomous agent need legal personhood, or can existing entities and human responsibility do the job? This roundtable examines what recognition would actually give an agent: the ability to hold assets, enter contracts, bear obligations and appear in a dispute. We’ll compare company wrappers with registry-based approaches and ask what safeguards must accompany any new legal status.

sessions.title: Privacy & Credentials
sessions.description: An onchain entity may need to prove who can act, whether a condition is met, or where funds came from without exposing its entire history. This roundtable explores credentials, selective disclosure, and confidential transactions as accountability tools. Who issues the proof, who can challenge or revoke it, and what should happen when a regulator or court needs more information?

sessions.title: Liability, Records & Justice
sessions.description: When an autonomous system causes harm, resolving the dispute depends on more than identifying a bug. This roundtable connects security failures, reliable records and access to justice: what evidence must survive, who can rely on it, and how responsibility becomes a remedy. Drawing on onchain security and government records, we’ll examine the path from incident to enforceable outcome.

sessions.title: Can a Fintech Let Users Judge Its Complaints? A Case Study
sessions.description:
Private companies, especially fintechs, handle large volumes of small-value customer complaints. Doing this through internal support or the courts is often slow, expensive and seen as biased in the company’s favour. This session looks at Lemon, an Argentine crypto app that sends some consumer complaints to an independent, crowdsourced juror panel. 
​
​We’ll cover:
- What kinds of disputes it’s used for and how the process works from start to finish
- How it fits alongside consumer protection law and existing complaint channels
- What it changes for user trust and for the company’s costs
- Its limits and open questions, such as enforceability, juror incentives and which cases shouldn’t go this route


It’s useful for anyone in fintech, compliance or legal ops who is weighing alternatives to traditional complaint handling.

sessions.title: From ODR to AI-Assisted Dispute Resolution: The Future of Arbitration and Mediation
sessions.description: Online dispute resolution (ODR) has moved arbitration and mediation onto digital platforms, and AI is now changing how disputes get resolved. Speaking from an Indian perspective, D. Saravanan, Chairman of the Council for National and International Commercial Arbitration, looks at where AI already helps, such as case triage, document review, outcome prediction and drafting settlements. The session also asks where human judgment still has to come first.

sessions.title: AI-Art’s Copyright Disputes
sessions.description: This research explores how generative AI models (such as Midjourney, Stability AI, and DALL-E 2) have brought a new wave of intellectual property rights (IPR) disputes to the forefront, categorised primarily into input infringement (unauthorised web-scraping and training on copyrighted artwork) and output infringement (producing content substantially similar to an artist's protected expression). The paper evaluates the insufficiencies of current legal routes (such as expensive and protracted class-action lawsuits) and non-legal tools (like Glaze, Nightshade, and robots.txt files). It then proposes a forward-looking AI Art IPR Dispute Resolution Model in Kleros, integrating decentralised blockchain-based arbitration with Digital Rights Management (DRM) systems.

sessions.description: Examines agent transaction liability by tracing a disputed service purchase through its entire chain—covering the principal, delegated mandates, policy checks, verification, and dispute remedies.
